Aluminium, paint, approx. 1600 cm x 172 cm x 8 cm. Installation view, TRACK, Ghent, 2012. Courtesy of the artist. TIMIșOARA .- The Art Encounters Foundation in Timișoara announces its collaboration with Philippe Van Cauteren, Artistic Director of the S.M.A.K. Museum in Ghent (Belgium), as appointed curator of the 7th edition of the Art Encounters Biennial, to be held in Timișoara (Romania). The Biennial will run from May 21 to July 4 2027, opening with a three-day program from May 21–23. The appointment also marks the beginning of a long-term strategic partnership between Art Encounters and S.M.A.K., opening a new chapter in the Biennial's development. Bringing together one of Europe's leading institutions dedicated to contemporary art and one of the region's most important biennials, the collaboration is structured around artistic co-production and professional exchange, with the aim of developing a sustainable model for conceiving and delivering a contemporary art biennial today. Philippe Van Cauteren’s involvement brings to the center of the 2027 edition a curatorial vision built around dialogue with artists and critical reflection on the role of the museum and the biennial in contemporary society. "The invitation to curate the Art Encounters Biennial 2027 is a great honor. I am delighted to contribute to this vital and unique project which promotes the visibility of art and artists through dialogue and collaboration. The opportunity to contribute to the legacy of the Biennial is a chance to learn, to discover, and to share both the local identity of Timișoara, and the constellation of relations that the working process brings. I am convinced that the Art Encounters Biennial 2027 will be more than an exhibition; it will also be a platform for national and international exchanges, including with S.M.A.K., among others." – Philippe Van Cauteren Van Cauteren has led S.M.A.K. (the Museum of Contemporary Art in Ghent) for over 15 years, making it one of the European institutions that have played an active role in supporting contemporary art in recent decades. Under his direction, the museum has developed an internationally relevant collection and initiated numerous collaborations with artists, biennials, and major institutions, including participation in the Venice Biennale. His curatorial practice is recognized for its closeness to artists and its ability to connect local scenes with international cultural networks. Philippe Van Cauteren has published, among others, the book "Letters to Artists," a compilation of letters he has written to artists over the past 15 years. "For us, working with Philippe Van Cauteren and S.M.A.K. represents a partnership grounded in genuine exchange, co-production, and professional development. At the same time, his appointment highlights a curatorial approach we strongly believe in—one that allows the central importance of art in our lives to be recognized by everyone, as a vital force in both personal and collective growth." – Diana Marincu, Artistic Director of the Art Encounters Foundation The Art Encounters Biennial is the flagship project of the Art Encounters Foundation and stands at the intersection between an experimental art festival and a contemporary art biennial. It is based on extensive curatorial research, engaging in a real dialogue with the historical and socio-cultural context of Timișoara. The Biennial’s mission is to become a creative meeting point for artists, communities, institutions, and ideas. Philippe Van Cauteren is trained as an art historian and sociologist. He is the artistic director of S.M.A.K. (Museum for Contemporary Art, Ghent, Belgium). In the past decades he has made exhibitions in Brazil, Chile, Iraq, Turkey, Nepal, Belgium. He was a.o. curator of the Belgian Pavilion (2013) and Iraq Pavilion (2015) in the Venice Biennial, and curator of the first Kathmandu Triennial (2017) in Nepal. In 2027 he will be curator of the Art Encounters Biennial in Timișoara, Romania. Art Encounters Biennial 2027 is funded by the City of Timișoara through the Centre for Projects, and it's organized in partnership with S.M.A.K Ghent. https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cw14.text: Image source, Getty Images By Sareen Habeshian Reporting from Los Angeles Published 4 hours ago Six Flags Magic Mountain, an amusement park in California, has announced it will permanently close a popular rollercoaster after more than 100 riders alleged they suffered brain injuries. The X2 rollercoaster, one of the park's main attractions, with long wait times to ride and seats that spin 360 degrees, has been closed since July. Six Flags said the ride had passed a range of safety tests, but that it had decided to retire it because it was "the right thing to do". The decision comes after lawsuits and news reports alleged that riders suffered brain injuries after riding X2. A law firm representing some of the plaintiffs said the decision had come "too late" for its clients. Announcing the closure on Tuesday, , external Six Flags Magic Mountain Park President Brian Oerding said: "Ride safety is a cornerstone of our business, and when we see guest confidence affected, we take it seriously." Dordick Law Corporation, who filed civil lawsuits against the park, said it had been contacted by about 400 people who alleged they had injuries they believed were caused by the ride. "They got on X2 expecting a thrill. Instead, they left with catastrophic brain injuries," the firm said in a statement. "Some needed emergency brain surgery. Some are still fighting to get their lives back." The law firm said that while it welcomed the closure of the ride to protect future guests, "it does nothing for the people who have already been hurt". Originally called X, the ride first opened in 2002 but was closed months later for repairs to design flaws, the Los Angeles Times reports. It was then closed again in 2007 to replace its trains with lighter versions. It reopened the following year as X2 and since then has been ridden by more than 16 million people, the park said. A law firm that represented the family of 22-year-old Christopher Hawley, who died after riding X2 in 2022, said the closure was not enough. While the Hawley family is "relieved to hear that Six Flags is finally closing the X2, it does not change the fact that Christopher Hawley was killed by a dangerous roller coaster that was allowed to operate for nearly two decades," attorney Brent Wisner of Wisner Baum LLP said in a statement to the BBC. Hawley's family settled a wrongful death suit with the theme park in August. "That tragedy cannot be undone," Wisner said, calling for legal reform, proactive regulation and proper governmental oversight. "We cannot rely on profit-centered corporations to do the right thing only after enough people have been hurt," he added. "We hope that whatever replaces the X2 is safe." https://artdaily.com/news/201118/Exhibit.text: Home Last Week Artists Architects Galleries Museums Photographers Photography PhotoGallery Games Subscribe Comments Search Contact Exhibition marks a century since Alan Turing's Dorset schooldays and his indelible legacy on the 20th and 21st centuries Today, Turing is famous not only for his role in breaking the Enigma code, but he is also widely regarded as the founder of modern computing and AI. DORSET .- To mark 100 years since Alan Turing (1912-1954) arrived at Sherborne School, a new exhibition explores the pioneering British polymath’s formative friendships, school years and ideas before his crucial role at Bletchley Park during WW2. Today, Turing is famous not only for his role in breaking the Enigma code, but he is also widely regarded as the founder of modern computing and AI. The exhibition, Turing Before Bletchley traces back to May 1926, when at the age of 13, Turing was enrolled at Sherborne School, then an independent boarding school in the picturesque Dorset market town, where he boarded at Westcott House. Turing’s first day of term coincided with the 1926 General Strike, but he was so determined to attend that he famously rode his bicycle 60 miles (97 km) from Southampton to Sherborne. If this wasn’t remarkable enough, Turing had already travelled alone from Dinard in France, where his family were living, taking the ferry from Saint-Malo to Southampton, from where he intended to travel by train to Sherborne. However, on arriving in England and discovering that no trains were running, Turing sent a telegram to his housemaster Geoffrey O’Hanlon at Westcott House informing him that he would be a day late arriving at Sherborne. Having brought his bicycle with him from France, he bought a map and set off for Sherborne. This extraordinary story and many others from his early life are brought together in a fascinating display of archive material, photographs, school reports, transcripts and correspondence. The Sherborne’s new exhibition looks beyond Turing the codebreaker, to explore the young man whose ideas and relationships developed during his school years in the town. Of course, as Turing is and always will be synonymous with Bletchley Park, Hut 8, and his vital codebreaking work, the exhibition will also give visitors a chance to see a rare replica of the Enigma machine at The Sherborne, placing Turing’s early life and personal story alongside the wider history of his wartime work, mathematics, computing and his extraordinary legacy. Offering further insights into Turing’s early life and thoughts, high-quality facsimiles of selected correspondence, including previously unseen private letters between Alan and Christopher Morcom, his close friend at Sherborne will help visitors to explore and understand some of the highly personal strands of Turing’s story. Turing Before Bletchley will be further accompanied by a programme of talks, family activities and codebreaking events throughout the autumn, including STEM workshops for children and special programming opportunities across the October half term holiday. Alongside the scientific story, The Sherborne will explore some unexpected cultural connections. These include Edward Elgar’s Enigma Variations (1898/99), a work created around a musical puzzle and portraits of the composer’s closest friends. Although unrelated to the Enigma machine, Elgar’s most famous work offers an intriguing parallel with Turing’s letters and the exhibition’s wider themes of friendship, hidden meaning, interpretation and unresolved questions. “Before Bletchley Park, before the Enigma machine and before Turing became one of the defining minds of the twentieth century, there was Sherborne,” says Liz Gilmore, CEO of The Sherborne. “Our new exhibition will also explore the meeting point between art, music, mathematics and early computing, reflecting The Sherborne’s wider ambition to bring different disciplines together and inspire curiosity.” Alan Turing was born on 23rd June 1912 in Maida Vale, London. His mother was Chief Engineer at the Madras Railway and his father was a Civil Servant. Turing did well at school and went on to study mathematics at Kings College - Cambridge, where he was awarded a first-class honour in 1934. He subsequently went on to obtain his PhD from the Department of Mathematics from Princeton in 1938. Alan Turing joined the GC&CS – the forerunner to GCHQ - in September 1939 to help with the code-breaking effort during WW2, working alongside Gordon Welchman (1906-1985). Turing was a leading cryptanalyst at Bletchley Park and spearheaded the effort in Hut 8 focusing on the German Naval Enigma, where he worked closely with Joan Clarke (1917-1996). Turing was inspired by those around him, using their knowledge and initiative as a foundation to develop further. In January 1940, Turing met with Polish counterparts who gave him the insights he needed to design the Bombe. The Bombe was the first special-purpose British cryptanalytic machine and made a major contribution to the exploitation of Enigma. The combination of the Bombe and the brilliant minds and perseverance of those working at Bletchley Park led to the breaking of Enigma. After working on Enigma, Turing moved to the US where he worked on investigating secure speech systems and helped with the development of what would become the US cipher machine SIGABA. After his return to the UK in 1943 he developed a portable secure voice scrambler (codenamed Delilah). His skills at finding and exploiting weaknesses in other people’s systems made him best placed to design new secure systems. In 1945, Turing moved on to work at the National Physical Laboratory in London. While there, he worked on the ACE (Automatic Computing Engine) which was the first detailed design of a stored-program computer. In 1948, Turing joined the Mathematics Department at Manchester University. A year later, he became Deputy Director of the Computing Machine Laboratory. Working with Max Newman (1897-1984), he led a team that produced Britain's first general-purpose stored programme computer (the Manchester Mark 1) and then the first commercial computer (the Ferranti Mark 1). In 1950, Turing turned his attention to artificial intelligence and proposed an experiment attempting to define a standard for a machine to be called “intelligent”, this became known as the Turing Test. In January 1952, Turing was prosecuted for indecency over his relationship with another man in Manchester. In March 1952, Turing pleaded guilty to the charges and was given a choice between imprisonment and probation; he chose probation which was conditional upon him undergoing hormonal treatment intended to reduce his libido. On the 8 June 1954, Turing took his own life. https://www.historyextra.com/membership/.text: Are these the world’s oldest cities? Inside the megasites that Soviet authorities didn’t want you to see Hilary Mitchell introduces the Cucuteni-Trypillia, archaeological megasites that rival Uruk and Çatalhöyük for the accolade of ‘world’s oldest city’, knowledge of which was suppressed by the Soviet Union for decades. But why? Hilary Mitchell Published: October 11, 2026 at 4:00 PM Save Share on facebook Share on twitter Share on whatsapp Email to a friend If you were taking a quiz and were asked what the ‘world’s oldest city’ is, you’d probably get a point for answering Uruk, the ancient metropolis in what is now Iraq. It’s thought that this famous site, renowned for its monumental architecture, administrative sophistication and early use of writing, may have had an impressive 40,000 residents by its final phase in 3100 BC. Ad At that time, Uruk was home to people who didn’t have to sully their noble hands by farming. They were true urbanites who obtained their food from the surrounding hinterland – one of the features that many archaeologists consider to be an essential characteristic of a city. Another site, Çatalhöyük in modern-day Turkey, also has a claim to the title of ‘world’s oldest city’, though it would appear quite strange to modern eyes: a streetless mass of houses clustered back-to-back with roof access into the buildings. Founded in around 7100 BC and abandoned in 5700 BC, it was certainly a significant and long-lasting settlement, as was Jericho in Palestine. Archaeologists have unearthed the remains of more than 20 successive settlements in Jericho, the first of which dates back 11,000 years to 9000 BC. By 7370 BC, Jericho was a well-established town of small, round mud brick houses surrounded by a 12-foot-high stone wall with a defensive tower. UNESCO describes Jericho as the “oldest fortified city in the world.” The existence of these famous and extremely well-documented sites gave rise to the belief that the first cities emerged in Mesopotamia, and that the area was, essentially, the cradle of urban civilisation. However, recent research has challenged that long-held assumption. Remains of an ancient temple wall in Busha, Ukraine. Archaeological exploration has uncovered new information about the world’s first cities | Credit: Dreamstime Are these really the world’s oldest cities? Around 6,500 years ago, an enigmatic society flourished across the forest-steppe expanse of present-day Ukraine, Moldova and Romania. Known as the Cucuteni-Trypillia culture, or – more poetically – as “the last great Chalcolithic civilization of Europe,” ( Mantu et al ., 1997) its people constructed vast settlements that more than rival – in both size and organisation – the other proto-cities mentioned above. The largest Cucuteni-Trypillia megasite is Talianki in Ukraine, which covered an area of around 450 hectares and is thought to have housed up to 21,000 inhabitants. Other significant megasites include Maidanetske (250 hectares/17,500 inhabitants), Dobrovody (250 hectares/16,200 inhabitants) and Nebelivka (275 hectares/15,000 inhabitants). Megasites like Talianki weren’t just a random agglomeration of buildings: they appear to have been as meticulously planned out as any mass-produced postwar British suburb, with rows of houses radiating in concentric circles around a central open area, which may have been a space for community gatherings, perhaps fulfilling a similar purpose to a Roman forum. Reconstruction of Talianki, the largest Cucuteni-Trypillia megasite. Archaeological research shows that such sites were precisely mapped out | Credit: Kenny Arne Lang Antonsen & Jimmy John Antonsen The discovery of the Cucuteni-Trypillia megasites In the 1960s, Russian military topographer Konstantin Shishkin was examining some aerial photographs of Ukraine when he noticed unusual shadows materialising on the ground in the vicinity of Kyiv. He saw ghostly rings in the soil, caused by differences in plant growth due to buried archaeological remains. In total, Shishkin identified what looked to be more than 250 examples of these strange shadows – all of them eerie traces of long-vanished structures. Subsequent excavations and research confirmed that these communities represented some of the earliest examples of large-scale, low-density urban planning. And while Mesopotamian cities such as Uruk were celebrated for their temples and palaces, these sites tell a different story. For more than 2,000 years, the Cucuteni-Trypillia culture made pots, hunted and gathered, farmed, and lived in huge settlements where all the houses were almost exactly the same size. There were no signs of palaces, monumental tombs, or, in fact, graves of any kind. No one knows what these people did with their dead, which makes it harder to construct a clear picture of their religious beliefs or rituals. A zoomorphic statuette with wheels from c.3950–3500 BC. Models like this have given insight into the Cucuteni-Tyrpillia culture – but little is known about their beliefs around death | Credit: Getty Images But the lack of grave goods for most of the culture’s history may itself shed some light on the society’s world view. Instead of being buried with their owners, metal objects may have – more practically – been melted down and reused. All houses were roughly five metres wide and up to 14 metres long. Constructed of wood and clay and resembling modern half-timbered buildings, they showed a striking degree of standardisation. “The architecture is reminiscent of Lego,” observed archaeologist Johannes Müller of Kiel University in Germany, who has studied the sites extensively since 2011. This equality and uniformity piqued the interest of Soviet authorities at the time, who saw in these sites an almost perfect example of an idealised past: a truly classless society in line with Marxist ideology. Speaking to the BBC in 2021, Mykhailo Videiko, an archaeologist at Borys Grinchenko Kyiv Metropolitan University in Ukraine, explained why the authorities later went out of their way to suppress further scientific research and cover up the discovery. Read more | An ancient mystery is hiding under one of Scotland's major archaeological sites – and it's about to be dug up It was thought that “Trypillia was a wonderful illustration of a pre-class, classless society or primitive communism,” said Videiko. “As archaeologists are digging more, they start discovering megasites of Trypillia civilisation. They start finding all these huge buildings. And the question arises: Could this all be done by a classless society?” he added. Some interpreted the large structures, some over 700 square metres in size, as temples. Others thought they were more likely to be storehouses for grain. Whatever they were, they didn’t align with the authorities’ vision of an ancient, social hierarchy-free Marxist utopia, so they cracked down on the project. Some archaeologists were convicted as being members of a terrorist spy organisation; others fled the country. Books that furthered the study of Trypillia were published elsewhere but, Videiko explained: “Those books never reached Ukraine. They were researching something but almost no one here knew about it. Those who knew, remained silent.” The renaissance of Cucuteni-Trypillia research In the mid-1990s, archaeologist Roland Fletcher drew global attention to an overlooked prehistoric phenomenon: vast Neolithic-Chalcolithic settlements in Eastern Europe that appeared to defy the usual constraints of early agricultural communities. His 1995 book The Limits of Settlement Growth describes the Cucuteni-Trypillia megasites as the sole known exception to his global model for the way in which all early settlements were limited in size and complexity. Roland Fletcher (right) above a trench during an excavation, 2008. In the 1990s, he brought attention to prehistoric sites that disrupted previous understandings of early communities | Credit: Alamy Fletcher’s analysis highlighted a critical point: the enormous scale of these sites, some covering hundreds of hectares, would have made it virtually impossible for all inhabitants to remain in regular, face-to-face contact. This suggested either a sophisticated level of internal organisation, perhaps with designated areas, or possibly an early form of writing that aided communication. A major step forward came in 2009, when a collaborative research team from Frankfurt and Kiel universities launched a comprehensive study of several key Cucuteni-Trypillia sites. These included Nebelivka, Talianki, Maidanetske and Dobrovody, among the most prominent mega-settlements, as well as the smaller site of Apolianka. This ambitious project, detailed in a 2014 issue of the European Journal of Archaeology , employed cutting-edge geophysical methods to investigate the sites more thoroughly than ever before using more advanced magnetic gradiometry. The Frankfurt-Kiel team were able to confirm that these settlements were laid out in concentric circles, suggesting an impressive degree of organisation. This suggests that all of the structures were carefully planned out before any construction began, strengthening the case that Talianki and similar megasites deserve to be called the oldest cities in history. Read more | The Amazon rainforest is hiding an ancient secret – and scientists now know what it is University of Kiel archaeologist Johannes Müller has put his cards on the table and confirmed that he considers them to be cities, saying: “When I started researching the Tripillia sites in 2012, I never thought I would call them ‘cities’.” Müller continued that now “that is beyond question for me. A city requires a concept. And here, planning is evident from the very beginning.” “The decisive factor for me is not that they are huge settlements, but that you no longer know the people who live 1.5 kilometers away in the same settlement,” he added. Why did the Cucuteni-Trypillia culture burn their houses? The Frankfurt-Kiel team’s research also confirmed a particularly baffling element of the megasite mystery: the fate of the ‘Lego’ houses themselves. Many appear to have been deliberately burned, often every 60 to 80 years, leaving behind squares of ash containing magnetic oxides. Some researchers suggest the burnings had a symbolic or ritual motive, perhaps linked to death or rebirth. Others think they served a more pragmatic purpose: perhaps hardening clay walls or clearing land for rebuilding. Mirjana Stevanovic, an archaeologist from Serbia, has argued that the structures inside the burned house horizon “were destroyed by deliberate burning and most likely for reasons of a symbolic nature.” A Trypillia scholar, Vikentiy Khvoyka, believes that the houses were burned down when their inhabitants passed away, turning them from dwellings of the living into what he called “homes of the dead.” However, Russian archaeologist Evgeniy Yuryevich Krichevski had a different take on the practice. He thought that the inhabitants weren’t destroying their homes, just reinforcing them. He believed that the heat of the flames would have hardened the clay walls into a ceramic surface, while the smoke would have fumigated the living space. A handmade ceramic lobate vessel from the Cucuteni-Trypillia culture. There are theories that communities burned their houses to turn clay walls into harder ceramic ones | Credit: Dreamstime In 2018, a team of Ukrainian and British archaeologists decided to put this theory to the test. They recreated two Cucuteni-Trypillia type houses, building them from scratch from the same clay and wood materials used thousands of years ago. Although wooden elements such as the roof were destroyed, the team found that the walls of both buildings were left intact, along with various clay items and ritual items the researchers had placed inside. Read more | These Iron Age bodies were all buried in the same bizarre way. What does it mean? What artefacts are associated with the Cucuteni-Trypillia people? Wherever Cucuteni-Trypillia people lived, archaeologists have found stylised, small female figurines, with distinctive geometric designs on their curvy bodies. In the 1970s, Lithuanian archaeologist Marija Gimbutas, working at UCLA, California, published several influential books suggesting that the female figures were goddesses, and that the Cucuteni-Trypillia people, along with other early societies of ‘Old Europe’, were led by women – though these days, Gimbutas’s work is considered to be highly speculative. However, whether it points to a wide-reaching, goddess-worshipping matriarchal culture or not, the material legacy of the Cucuteni-Trypillia culture is deeply compelling. Cucuteni–Trypillia pottery in particular – yellow-hued and decorated in stunning swirling patterns and vibrant colours – speaks of a deeply sophisticated artistic tradition. A female figurine created during the time of the Cucuteni-Trypillia culture. There has been speculation that such feminine art indicated matriarchal values in that society | Credit: Getty Images Archaeologist Mykhailo Videiko has explained that the people of Trypillia “managed to implement almost all technological innovations of their time,” using kilns that were very advanced for that period. In an attempt to raise awareness about the extraordinary craftsmanship of her ancestors, in 2021, Ukrainian fashion designer Svitlana Bevza created a line of Trypillia-influenced clothing and jewellery as a way of celebrating this – as the Frankfurt-Kiel team put it – “persistently overlooked” ancient civilisation. Bevza told the BBC she found it unjust that “this great culture is not that well-known in the world, as Egyptian, for instance. There was no voice to the world who could talk about this culture.” In the five years since she created her evocative collection, more light has been shed on these extraordinary settlements, and they are finally beginning to get the recognition they deserve. Ad In a field where terminology is often debated and definitions evolve, one thing is becoming clearer: the Cucuteni-Trypillia culture – once viewed as peripheral to early urban development – is now rightfully taking centre stage in our understanding of how cities first emerged. https://vietnamnews.vn/opinion/1802924/g.text: Great solidarity festival to strengthen cohesion among Vietnamese communities in Europe: ambassador PRAGUE — The first Việt Nam Great National Solidarity Festival in Europe, scheduled to take place in Prague on October 31 and November 1, will strengthen solidarity among Vietnamese communities abroad, honour their contributions and promote friendship between Việt Nam and European countries, including the Czech Republic, a Vietnamese diplomat has said. In an interview granted to the Vietnam News Agency correspondents in Prague ahead of the event, Vietnamese Ambassador to the Czech Republic Dương Hoài Nam said the festival will convey a message of unity, attachment to the Fatherland and shared responsibility for the future. He stressed that overseas Vietnamese (OVs) remain an inseparable part of the nation, with love for the homeland and efforts to preserve the Vietnamese language, cultural identity and family traditions serving as enduring bonds. The event will also enable Vietnamese communities across Europe to share experiences, strengthen links among associations and mobilise collective efforts for national development. Amid global uncertainties, solidarity is increasingly important to helping OVs support one another, integrate into host societies and promote cooperation between Việt Nam and other countries, Nam stressed. The diplomat said the Czech Republic is a fitting venue for the inaugural festival, given its large, dynamic and well-integrated Vietnamese community and its longstanding ties with Việt Nam as a strategic partner. Over generations, Vietnamese people in the country have helped foster people-to-people exchanges, economic cooperation and a positive image of Việt Nam. He expressed his hope that the festival will become a catalyst for closer ties among Vietnamese generations in Europe, particularly young people, encouraging them to take pride in their origins, proactively preserve cultural values and practically contribute to both Việt Nam and their host societies. Assessing the Confederation of Vietnamese Associations in Europe (CVAE) over the past decade, Nam said it has become an important platform for connecting Vietnamese communities, coordinating activities and promoting the preservation of the Vietnamese language, cultural identity and traditions. Its homeland-orientated initiatives, support for people in Việt Nam and engagement with communities in host societies also reflect OVs' attachment to their homeland and sense of responsibility. He stressed that the confederation’s role is growing as Vietnamese communities in Europe become more diverse in age, professions, living conditions and levels of integration. To strengthen community ties, the ambassador called for enhancing solidarity while respecting differences and ensuring harmonious interests, boosting more dialogue, coordination and experience sharing among associations, and promoting broader participation by respected community members and other individuals. Engaging young people should also be a priority, he said, noting that Vietnamese people born and raised in the Czech Republic and elsewhere in Europe possess advantages in language skills, knowledge, technology and international connectivity. Associations should create more opportunities for them to participate in community activities, assume leadership roles and organise cultural, educational, charitable and youth exchange programmes. Practical initiatives, including Vietnamese language classes, summer camps, visits to the roots and exchanges with young people in the homeland, could help young OVs deepen their understanding of the country's history, culture and people, Nam said, adding that cooperation in education, science, technology, entrepreneurship and innovation should also be expanded to enable OV youth to contribute their expertise. Closer coordination among Vietnamese associations, representative agencies and organisations across Europe is also needed. The diplomat said that while previous generations have built communities through hard work, perseverance and mutual support, younger generations could carry these values forward through knowledge, creativity and international integration. Connecting the experience of previous generations with the aspirations of younger ones is therefore essential to sustaining national solidarity. Describing the homeland as a repository of memories, roots and values that shape identity, Nam said geographical distance could not diminish Vietnamese people's affection for or sense of responsibility towards the Fatherland. He expressed his hope that the festival will further strengthen solidarity among Vietnamese communities in the Czech Republic and across Europe, inspiring them to build on previous generations' achievements and contribute to the development of both Việt Nam and their host societies. — VNA/VNS Opinion Mutual trust, commitment to cooperation tie Việt Nam and Japan: expert Opinion OP-ED: Optimising cultural strength, reinforcing great national unity from grassroots Opinion Việt Nam’s top leader seeks more investment, cooperation from Japan: Japanese media Opinion Aligning education with in-demand skills key to UK-Việt Nam partnership: ambassador Opinion Japan, Việt Nam seek to elevate comprehensive strategic partnership during top leader Tô Lâm's visit Opinion Top Vietnamese leader’s Japan visit expected to open up new areas of cooperation: Ambassador Opinion How Việt Nam grows matters just as much as how fast When Việt Nam took its seat in 1977, it was a country still healing from war.
